slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open the lecture by separating two ideas that students often blend together: a curve can have ordinary acceleration in space and still be straight on the surface. The chapter starts from that local straightness test and then builds toward equations, conservation laws, variational meaning, and coordinates. Emphasize that the deck uses the chapter notebook as its computational companion, while the source pages give the mathematical order of topics.

slides.label: Route
slides.notes: Use this slide as the hour map. The audience should know that the lecture is not a list of examples but a chain: one differential condition becomes an ODE, the ODE gives examples, symmetry gives a conserved quantity, and the variational viewpoint explains why these paths are candidates for shortest curves. The final move is conceptual: geodesics are not just curves on a surface, they can become coordinates for the surface.

slides.label: Definition
slides.notes: Spend time on the decomposition because it is the conceptual hinge of the chapter. The ambient acceleration vector is not required to be zero; a great circle on a sphere accelerates toward the center in three-dimensional space. What vanishes is the part of acceleration that lies in the tangent plane, so the surface sees the curve as unforced. This is the differential-geometric version of a straight line.

slides.label: Equations
slides.notes: Present the equation as the coordinate translation of zero covariant acceleration. Students do not need to memorize every Christoffel expression at this moment; they need to understand that the symbols are determined by the first fundamental form and its derivatives. The second-order nature is important because it explains why a point and velocity determine the local curve. This also prepares the examples on the sphere, cylinder, and surfaces of revolution.

slides.label: Sphere
slides.notes: Use the sphere because it turns the definition into a familiar picture. A great circle is not straight in space, but its acceleration points normal to the sphere, so the tangential component vanishes. The displayed formula gives the geometric reason: the curve stays in a two-dimensional plane through the origin. Contrast this with a latitude circle, whose ambient acceleration is not purely surface-normal unless the latitude is a great circle.

slides.label: Cylinder
slides.notes: This example is a good place to say that geodesics are intrinsic. The cylinder can be cut and flattened without stretching, and in the flat sheet geodesics are ordinary straight lines. When the sheet is wrapped back up, those lines appear as circles, generators, or helices depending on slope. This demonstrates why a curve that looks spatially complicated may still be locally shortest and straight on the surface.

slides.label: Clairaut
slides.notes: Frame Clairaut's relation as Noether's theorem in elementary clothing: rotational symmetry creates a conserved momentum. The formula says that a geodesic trades radius against angle. Near a narrow waist, a path with too much angular momentum cannot keep moving inward, so it turns around. This gives students a prediction tool before they solve any explicit differential equation.

slides.label: Parallels
slides.notes: This slide turns the Clairaut discussion into concrete curve families. Meridians are geodesics for a structural reason: the surface has a reflection symmetry that keeps the meridian fixed, and uniqueness prevents the geodesic from leaving it. Parallels are subtler because most circles around the axis want to drift toward a nearby radius. The critical-radius condition tells students exactly which parallels can be geodesics.

slides.label: Shortest
slides.notes: This is where straightest and shortest meet. A shortest path with fixed endpoints cannot be improved by any small endpoint-fixed deformation, so the first variation of length must vanish. The Euler-Lagrange conclusion is the geodesic equation. Stress the logical direction: every sufficiently short minimizing segment is geodesic, but a geodesic may stop minimizing after it passes a cut point or conjugate behavior.

slides.label: Local Not Global
slides.notes: This caution prevents a common misconception. A geodesic is the critical curve for length, and locally it is the path produced by the straightest possible motion. But critical points need not be global minima. On a sphere the long arc of a great circle is still geodesic, even though the complementary arc is shorter. This motivates the exponential map and the cut-locus picture in the next part of the lecture.

slides.label: Exponential Map
slides.notes: Define the exponential map as a way to repackage the initial-value theorem. Instead of listing all geodesics through a point, we let each tangent vector tell us which geodesic to follow and how far. For small vectors this behaves like a coordinate chart. The sphere shows why one must be careful at larger radius: every direction of length pi from the north pole reaches the same south pole.

slides.label: Geodesic Polar Coordinates
slides.notes: Geodesic coordinates are the payoff of the exponential map. Starting from a point, the radial coordinate is literal arclength along a geodesic, and the angular coordinate records the initial direction. The metric form shown on the slide expresses Gauss' lemma: radial and angular directions are orthogonal. This is a powerful simplification because it adapts the coordinate grid to intrinsic distance.

slides.label: Gauss Lemma
slides.notes: Do not try to prove every analytic detail here; use the slide to explain the mechanism. The radial direction changes how far along the same initial direction we travel, while the angular direction changes the initial direction without changing the radius. The first variation formula says these two motions are orthogonal at the endpoint. This is why geodesic circles behave like ordinary circles to first order around their center.

slides.label: Curvature Link
slides.notes: This slide is a bridge, not a new theorem-heavy section. Once radial geodesics become coordinate lines, the remaining metric coefficient tells us how distance changes around the angular direction. That coefficient will later encode curvature through how rapidly nearby geodesics converge or diverge. This prepares students to see geodesics as measuring devices, not only as paths.

slides.label: Proof Dependency
slides.notes: Use this as a mid-lecture consolidation slide. The chapter's ideas are tightly connected, and students benefit from seeing the proof graph rather than treating each theorem as isolated. The acceleration split gives the definition, the coordinate equation gives computable existence, examples build intuition, and the first variation gives the length interpretation. The exponential map and geodesic coordinate theorem then synthesize local ODE data into a coordinate system.

slides.label: Worked Checks
slides.notes: Point students to the notebook as a way to audit the theory. The numerical checks are not there to replace the proofs; they expose the quantities that the proofs claim should remain zero or constant. The sphere ODE checks great-circle behavior, the cylinder verifies local isometry intuition, and the Clairaut lab turns symmetry into a measurable invariant. The first-variation experiment helps distinguish geodesic stationarity from arbitrary curve families.

slides.label: Exercises
slides.notes: These prompts are designed to be solved from the lecture rather than from copied textbook exercises. The sphere check reinforces the distinction between ambient acceleration and tangential acceleration. The cylinder check makes intrinsic geometry visible through a local isometry. The Clairaut prediction asks students to reason qualitatively from a conserved quantity, which is often more valuable than solving a complete ODE.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter thesis. The entire chapter can be remembered as the unfolding of one condition: zero tangential acceleration. From that condition we get equations, examples, conserved quantities, variational consequences, and coordinates. The next natural question is how curvature influences the behavior of these geodesic families, especially how fast nearby geodesics separate or focus.
